title: Characterization and empirical correction of a spatially coherent spectral artifact in Gemini/GMOS-N IFU observations
summary: We report a recurring spectral artifact identified in observations obtained with the integral field unit (IFU) of the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on the Gemini North telescope (GMOS-N). The artifact appears as a vertically aligned structure in reconstructed images of the IFU field of view, associated with a specific group of fibers and exhibiting a broad spectral feature around 8000~\AAng. Similar features were repeatedly identified in observations of different astronomical targets obtained between 2020 and 2022 using the R150 grating in the two-slit IFU mode. Taking advantage of the reproducibility of the artifact in the fiber and wavelength domains, we develop an empirical correction method in which the artifact is modeled as the product of a common spectral profile and a fiber-dependent amplitude distribution, with an overall normalization determined independently for each exposure. The artifact template is constructed from observations in which the affected fibers are largely separated from the astronomical source and subsequently applied to independent observations in which the artifact overlaps the source. The correction substantially suppresses the artificial spatial structure in the reconstructed images. Although the physical origin of the artifact remains unidentified, we present its observational characteristics and correction procedure to facilitate the identification and treatment of similar features by other GMOS-IFU users.

title: Halo spin-axis correlations in IllustrisTNG: Lagrangian-to-Eulerian separation mapping, baryonic effects, and redshift-space distortions
summary: We investigate correlations of halo and stellar spin axes in the TNG300 volume of the IllustrisTNG simulations and compare them with a model based on linear tidal torque theory (LTTT). Dark matter (DM) halo spin axes at $z = 0$ exhibit positive correlations as a function of Lagrangian pair separation. The LTTT-based model describes their separation dependence well, with weak variation in the fitted amplitude across mass thresholds. A Lagrangian-to-Eulerian separation mapping based on the conditional distributions of initial separations at fixed present-day separation, measured directly from the simulations, allows the model to reproduce the overall trends in both real and redshift space without additional fitting. The hydrodynamic and DM-only runs generally show similar DM halo spin-axis correlations, although the DM-only run exhibits a steeper rise at small real-space separations. In the hydrodynamic run, stellar spin-axis correlations are consistent with the same Lagrangian form as their DM halo counterparts, but with approximately 60% of the DM correlation amplitudes. Positive stellar correlations persist in both real and redshift space, and the mapped model captures their separation dependence. Initial spin-axis correlations of protohalos are substantially stronger than their present-day counterparts at the same Lagrangian separations, consistent with subsequent nonlinear spin evolution weakening these correlations. These results suggest that present-day halo and stellar spin-axis correlations retain signatures of the initial tidal field and that their general behavior can be understood through LTTT-based modeling combined with pair-separation mapping.

title: AT2024dky as an Off-nuclear Tidal Disruption Event Candidate
summary: Through a retrospective search for tidal disruption events (TDEs) in the ZTF archives agnostic to their location within their host galaxies, we identify AT2024dky/ZTF24aagksvd as a promising off-nuclear TDE candidate. At $z=0.0592$, it lies at a projected offset of $3.72^{\prime\prime}$ (4.26 kpc) from the center of a massive ($M_{\rm gal}\sim10^{11}\,M_\odot$), quiescent galaxy. We present early-time ZTF and ATLAS optical photometry and late-time follow-up observations with Keck-I/LRIS, VLA, EP, and Chandra. With $M_{g,\rm peak}=-18.50$ mag, AT2024dky exhibits persistently blue color ($g-r\sim-0.1$ mag) through 80 d after peak. At $δt=858$ d, Keck reveals $M_{u'}=-13.07\pm0.09$ mag and $M_R > -14.15$ mag. At $δt=866$ d, VLA detects the transient at $νL_{ν,10\,\rm GHz}=(1.26\pm0.17)\times10^{38}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$. The combination of early photometric evolution, detected late-time radio and UV emission strongly favor a TDE interpretation. The properties of its host galaxy also bear remarkable similarities to the parent galaxies of known off-nuclear TDEs. Based on the low values of peak-time and late-time UV/optical luminosities, we favor a black hole mass of $\sim 10^5$--$10^6 M_\odot$. Together, these observations strongly favor an off-nuclear TDE.

title: Anisotropic Fluid Inhomogeneous Cosmology
summary: We propose a new framework for inhomogeneous cosmology based on General Relativity sourced by an anisotropic fluid. The model is parametrized by a single input function, the radial Misner--Sharp mass distribution at different redshifts, and admits exact solutions to Einstein's equations. Going beyond the standard assumption of small metric perturbations, it provides a fully relativistic framework to describe the non-linear regime of cosmic structure formation. The Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) cosmology is recovered both at early times and -- on large scales only -- at late times. Our Anisotropic Fluid Inhomogeneous Cosmology (AFIC) model provides a natural mechanism through which matter inhomogeneities give rise to late-time acceleration. The extensive term driving this effect does not enter the exact metric solution and therefore does not contribute to the local gravitational potential. Rather, it emerges as a genuinely large-scale effect induced by the inhomogeneous distribution of matter at late times. This mechanism may provide a physical interpretation of the results from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI). Finally, we present a simple analytical realization of the model and use it to provide an estimate of the present-day effective dark energy density.

title: Photometric Uncertainty Correction for Time-Domain Surveys: Vera C. Rubin Data Preview 2 Case Study
summary: Time-domain science, from variability detection to supernova cosmology, relies on accurate photometric uncertainties. We present a data-driven, catalog-level method to validate and improve the photometric uncertainties reported by time-domain surveys. The analysis is based on transforming light curves of non-variable objects into mean-variance whitened signals. We then estimate a correction to the uncertainties by matching the distribution of the whitened signals of all objects to the standard normal distribution, which they ought to follow when the uncertainties are correct. The correction can be modeled as a function of each measurement's flux, reported uncertainty, and available observational metadata, and can be applied to measurements of both non-variable and variable objects. Applied to the Rubin Observatory Data Preview 2 (DP2), the method shows that the uncertainties of bright sources are underestimated by up to a factor of five. The inferred corrections correspond to a magnitude error floor of about 10 mmag for both direct-image and difference-image photometry, decreasing to about 6 mmag in deeper fields. We provide the corrected uncertainties as part of the Rubin DP2 HATS catalogs.

title: Acoustic Priors from the Latest Cosmic Microwave Background Data
summary: We revisit the physics of the acoustic peaks and illustrate how early-Universe information in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) can be disentangled from late-time signatures imprinted by gravitational lensing and the integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect. Applying this separation to Planck PR4, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 temperature and polarization data combined with the joint lensing reconstruction, we update the model-independent constraints on the angular acoustic scale and the physical densities, $100θ_*=1.04100\pm0.00021$, $ω_{\rm b}=(2.2440\pm0.0099)\times10^{-2}$, and $ω_{\rm bc}=0.1410\pm0.0011$. These constraints are consistent with the previous Planck PR4-only analysis and remain stable for extended late-time cosmologies beyond $Λ$CDM. Adding ACT DR6 to the combination favors a higher $ω_{\rm b}$ and, through their correlation, a higher primordial tilt $n_{\rm s}$ than PR4 alone. The reconstructed lensing spectrum exceeds that of $Λ$CDM, with two features near $L\simeq50$ and $L\sim10^3$, and the excess is reduced when WMAP replaces the Planck primary spectra. Marginalizing over the lensing-induced peak smoothing, rather than tying it to the late-time model, lowers the preference of the CMB and DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) for $w_0w_a$CDM over $Λ$CDM from $3.0σ$ to $1.9σ$, or from $3.2σ$ to $2.4σ$ when Union3.1 supernovae are added. We further use the acoustic prior to predict BAO distances from CMB data alone under several late-time expansion histories, testing their consistency with DESI measurements assuming standard pre-recombination physics.

title: CHEX-MATE: Probing the thermal$-$non-thermal connection in radio halo clusters with LoTSS-DR2
summary: The main baryonic component of galaxy clusters is in the form of a hot plasma observed in the X-rays. In addition, clusters host a non-thermal component (relativistic particles and magnetic fields) which is studied mainly via radio telescopes and is dynamically coupled to the thermal plasma. These two components evolve together within the system and are subject to both micro and macro-physical processes which can be traced only with deep and detailed observations. We present the first homogeneous spatially resolved radio--X-ray study of 18 radio halo clusters combining CHEX-MATE and the LOFAR Two metre Sky Survey DR2. Radio ($I_R$) and X-ray ($I_X$) surface brightness are clearly correlated (Spearman coefficient $r_s \ge 0.5$), following a typically sublinear $I_R-I_X$ relation ($67 \pm 5\%$ of the sample) that appears to be independent of other cluster properties, although a tentative trend with mass/redshift may be worth exploring with larger samples. When inspecting such a relation as a function of the radius, we observe a variety of behaviours, which suggest that the interplay between the thermal and non-thermal plasma components varies with radius. We find the averaged slope profile of dynamically disturbed clusters to be consistent with expectations from turbulent re-acceleration models where a constant ratio between cosmic-ray electron and thermal energy densities is assumed. Differently, less perturbed clusters require an increasing cosmic-ray-to-thermal energy ratio with radius. Finally, we show that radio halo surface-brightness profiles can be effectively rescaled using X-ray information and theoretical expectations. This procedure significantly reduces their scatter and reveals common underlying trends based on the cluster dynamics, resembling what is observed for the thermal ICM, and strengthening the idea of a strong interplay between these two plasma components.

title: Superfit: A Supernova Spectral Classification Tool with Host-Galaxy Decomposition
summary: Superfit is a an open-source tool for automated spectroscopic classification of supernovae that accounts for redshift, reddening, and host-galaxy contamination. Here we present the latest version, which has been rewritten in Python and is now available as a web-based application. A user uploads an observed spectrum, and Superfit uses a curated library of transient and galaxy spectra to perform a simultaneous fit of transient and host galaxy spectra, while adjusting for color and redshift. In contrast to machine-learning algorithms, Superfit uses a least squares fitting approach, which is reproducible, verifiable, and understandable to users. The user may specify the binning of the spectra, set redshift and reddening limits, phase information, and restrict host galaxy and supernova templates for fitting. A new, expanded template library includes modern transient subclasses and associated observational metadata. A modern browser-based interface allows users to configure fitting parameters, visualize spectra, monitor fitting progress, and interactively inspect and compare ranked candidate matches and their individual components. We describe the fitting methodology, template library, software architecture, and web interface, and demonstrate its capabilities through classification examples.

title: 3D Shape Recovery of Human-Made Space Objects from Light Curves with Image Denoisers as Priors
summary: This study presents a denoiser-regularized framework for recovering the three-dimensional convex shapes of human-made space objects from unresolved light curves. These shape estimates support object characterization for space situational awareness and mission support. Conventional methods for recovering the extended Gaussian image (EGI) using nonnegative least squares and directional refinement can discard surface-normal information needed to represent curved surfaces. The proposed framework represents the EGI as an area image on an equirectangular grid and recovers it in a randomly rotated frame using the plug-and-play alternating direction method of multipliers with a domain-adapted DRUNet denoiser. It then reconstructs a convex polytope from the recovered area image using scale-invariant support optimization with analytical gradients and volume normalization. Across seven faceted and curved shapes, with 10 runs per condition, the proposed method increases mean convex-hull intersection over union (IoU) from 0.615 for the baseline to 0.872 at a signal-to-noise ratio of 30 dB. Mean Hausdorff distance decreases from 0.198 to 0.050, and mean Chamfer distance decreases from 0.167 to 0.041. All three metrics improve for six of the seven shapes. The proposed method also retains much of its accuracy under noise, with mean IoU decreasing from 0.881 for noiseless measurements to 0.854 at 20 dB.

title: phenjax: the IMRPhenomT waveform family in JAX for accelerated analyses on CPUs and GPUs
summary: We present phenjax, a JAX implementation of the precessing time-domain IMRPhenomT family of models for the gravitational wave signal emitted in compact binary coalescence. The code keeps the structure of its reference Python implementation, phenomxpy, and reproduces, on average, its polarizations to a few $\times 10^{-12}$ of the peak strain for all the models, aligned-spin and precessing. The waveform models now take advantage of the JAX construction: compiled once per array shape, vectorized over events (batching), differentiable and executed on CPUs or GPUs with the same source code. Different additional features address the cost of long signals and of heterogeneous populations in a batch. On one NVIDIA H100, for the precessing TPHM model on LISA-mass populations, phenjax is 3 to 6 times faster than phenomxpy when both codes evaluate one event at a time and 20 to 30 times faster when phenjax evaluates the events in batches of 8. We estimate that, for waveform generation, one GPU does the work of 1300 to 2700 cores of a current CPU node at 25 to 45 times less energy per waveform. As a backend of a global-fit LISA massive black hole pipeline, performed on the Sangria dataset, phenjax recovers the same posteriors as the other waveform backends at a lower computational cost. In a comparison with phentax, the wall time was 13 minutes instead of 21.

title: Optical Light-Curve Broadening in the Redback Binary PSR J2215+5135
summary: Spider millisecond pulsars offer a direct route to constrain neutron-star masses, including candidates above two solar masses, via optical light-curve modeling of the irradiated companion. This assumes stable irradiation. We report new $g'r'i'$ photometry of the redback PSR~J2215+5135 from the Iranian National Observatory in 2024 and compare it with the 2014 data of \citet{linares2018peering}. Peak brightness and orbital period are unchanged within uncertainties, but the light-curve wings are significantly broader in 2024, as the local deviations exceed $3σ$ on the rising branch in all filters, with an additional $i'$-band excess on the falling branch, giving a global permutation-test significance of $4.26σ$. A single-hot-spot model fits the 2024 data better than a spot-free one, but systematic residuals remain. The broader wings are reproduced only through correlated shifts in the spot, inclination, filling factor and companion temperature, which we regard as model compensation, not physics. An extended, variable heating component may also fit. The best-fit spot temperature differs between epochs by about $1060$\,K, comparable to its model dependence (about $900$\,K between two codes for 2014), so we do not interpret this as physical. Two epochs cannot show whether the change is gradual, sudden or short-lived. The inferred neutron-star mass depends on the spot treatment: $2.13^{+0.16}_{-0.13}\,M_\odot$ for 2014 with a hot spot, and $M_\mathrm{NS}=1.95^{+0.11}_{-0.07}\,M_\odot$ for 2024. These agree within about $1σ$, but come from differently shaped light curves, and the statistical uncertainties exclude heating-prescription systematics.

title: Modeling the LISA response in the time-frequency domain
summary: Time-frequency methods are a promising approach to LISA data analysis. This paper presents a model for the LISA response directly in the time-frequency domain using the Wilson-Daubechies-Meyer (WDM) transformation. The implementation is vectorized using JAX and can efficiently evaluate the response for batches of signals, achieving white-noise mismatches of $\sim 10^{-9}$ compared to existing implementations of the LISA one-arm response. Our results demonstrate that the LISA response can be modeled accurately and efficiently in the time-frequency domain, providing an important component of an end-to-end time-frequency LISA analysis framework.

title: The tangled warp of the Milky Way II: The red clump
summary: The Milky Way's disc is warped in a way that varies depending on the age of the population considered. We, for the first time, trace that kinematics of the warp in red clumps stars. This means that our sample is drawn from a consistent population across the disc, composed of standard candles that allow for precise distance estimates but, unlike samples of Cepheid variables, is relatively old. We find that, consistent with other populations, the red-clump warp is precessing at ${\sim}12\;{\rm km}\,{\rm s}^{-1}\,{\rm kpc}^{-1}$, comparable to the angular velocity of stars around the Galaxy in the outer reaches of the disc. Unlike younger populations, the kinematic signature is offset from that which we would expect given the stellar positions. This reinforces the conclusion that the Milky Way's warp is dynamically evolving, making this a necessary property of any model that seeks to explain its creation.

title: enCHASE: A pipeline for the calibration and analysis of CHASE/HIS observations
summary: We present 'enCHASE', an open-source pipeline for the calibration and analysis of H$α$ and Fe I 6569 Å observations from the Chinese H$α$ Solar Explorer (CHASE), addressing the lack of a public, documented tool for correcting residual instrumental effects in the mission's Level-1 data. The pipeline performs full-disk spatial registration, sub-field stabilization via correlation tracking and optical flow, wavelength offset correction, radiometric calibration against a high-resolution reference atlas, and stray-light correction. We demonstrate the method on six regions of different activity within one full-disk time series, including quiet Sun, a filament, a sunspot, a plage, a prominence, and an X1.2 flare. For reductions with both lines, we achieve a sub-pixel residual pointing error for tracked sub-fields, a wavelength zero-point that is stable to 1.2 mÅ (0.05 km\,s$^{-1}$), and an intensity calibration uncertainty of about 1\% of the continuum. When using only H$α$, we reach slightly higher uncertainties and therefore recommend the use of both lines in the reduction.

title: No Cluster Left Behind I: Joint Mass Calibration for Dark Energy Survey and South Pole Telescope Clusters
summary: Multiwavelength observations of galaxy clusters are among the most promising probes of the growth of structure and dark energy. Optically identified clusters have a high number density and can thus probe the halo mass function well into the group regime, but their weak-lensing mass calibration suffers from a selection bias induced by line-of-sight projection effects. Clusters detected via their intracluster medium (ICM) -- through X-ray emission or the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect (SZe) -- are less affected by such selection biases, but current survey sensitivity restricts ICM-selected samples to high-mass systems. Previous multiwavelength analyses tend to limit to clusters with millimeter detections and thus to the high-mass population. In this paper, we propose a flexible modeling framework in which all clusters from multiwavelength surveys can be combined and modeled, even if they are detected in only one survey. As a pilot study, we jointly model richness and lensing of clusters from the Dark Energy Survey and the SZe signal from the South Pole Telescope. This approach yields precise cluster mass calibration while self-consistently constraining optical selection biases. We have found a $\sim$20% bias in the large-scale lensing signal of clusters selected by richness, and a bias ranging from $\sim-20$% at low richness to zero at high richness for clusters selected by both richness and SZe. Compared to current approaches, this framework is highly scalable and readily extensible, paving the way for the full utilization of multiwavelength cluster data in next-generation surveys.

title: A comparison of two- and one-fluid dust solvers for dusty, supersonic turbulence
summary: We model 3 and 10 $μ$m dust grains in supersonic, turbulent molecular cloud conditions to compare two different numerical methods solving dust coupled to gas through a drag term. One method models dust and gas as two separate species (two fluid) and the other the combination of dust and gas as a single mixture (one fluid) using the diffusion approximation. Simulations are performed in a 3D periodic box using the Phantom code. The gas probability distributions are consistent with a lognormal distribution for both methods and grain sizes. The dust distributions are different in the two methods, showing discrepancies particularly in regions of low density. The most significant difference between the two methods is in the dust-to-gas ratio distributions. Both methods peak at the mean dust-to-gas ratio of 0.01, but the two-fluid method has wider distributions than the one-fluid method suggesting excess dust concentration in dense filaments. Filaments are where the one-fluid method results are most accurate. The narrowing of the one-fluid distribution is also caused by the stopping time limiter used to maintain the terminal velocity approximation. This artificially makes the mixture more coupled in low-density regions. Our overall conclusion is that both methods are viable for the study of dust in molecular clouds, but that the correct method should be chosen based on the numerical Stokes number regime of the calculation to avoid numerical artifacts.

title: The Splash population confined to the Milky Way bar region
summary: We investigate the chemo-dynamical properties of in-situ stars in the Galactic bar region (central $5$ kpc), specifically the inner Galactic counterpart of the solar-neighbourhood Splash population (in situ halo). We use a sample of APOGEE DR17 red giants with Gaia astrometry and AstroNN distances, and separate bulge/bar stellar populations dynamically using a normalised time-averaged bar-frame angular momentum, $\mathcal{V}_φ$. Chemo-dynamical maps in the $\mathcal{V}_φ$-[Fe/H] plane reveal a pronounced extension of the bar population towards $\mathcal{V}_φ<0$ (non-bar-following orbits) within $-1.0<{\rm [Fe/H]}<-0.3$, characterised by high eccentricities, large $z_{\rm max}$ and an extended spheroidal orbit density distribution, and accounting for $\sim 30\%$ of all stars at these metallicities. These $\mathcal{V}_φ<0$ stars have [Mg/Fe] and [Al/Fe] abundances similar to those of stars on ${\rm x_1}$ orbits at the same [Fe/H], and they match the solar-neighbourhood Splash in its metallicity and abundance ratio distributions. We therefore refer to them as the $\textit{central Splash}$. The presence of a significant central Splash underscores the role of the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger in the early history of the Galaxy. We find a similar, weaker extension in the $\mathcal{V}_φ$-[Fe/H] maps for extremely metal-rich stars, which are confined to the bulge. At metallicities [Fe/H] $<0.3$, we find no additional classical bulge population in these maps beyond the central Splash and proto-Galactic populations $-$ the high-$α$ bulge appears to have evolved from the early high-$α$ disc.

title: Tipping the scales in Blue Jay: Dust energy balance overpredicts IR luminosity in galaxies at $z\sim2$
summary: The spectral energy distribution (SED) of a galaxy encodes vital information about its chemical composition, stellar populations, and dust content. To model the infrared emission, many modern SED-fitting codes rely on dust energy balance, which assumes that all energy absorbed by dust in the UV-optical is equal to the energy emitted by dust in the infrared regime. However, few studies have been carried out to test the validity of this assumption at high redshift, where direct infrared observations are sparse. In this work, we perform aperture photometry in 111 galaxies from the Blue Jay survey ($1.7 < z < 3.5$) using public JWST/MIRI observations from the PRIMER, COSMOS-Web and COSMOS-3D surveys. Focusing on a subsample of 89 star-forming galaxies, we reconstruct best-fit SED model spectra from Prospector using only HST and NIRCam photometry and compare the predicted mid-infrared fluxes to the measured MIRI photometry. We find that mid-infrared fluxes are systematically overpredicted by about 10% at 7.7$μ$m up to a factor of $\sim3$ at 21$μ$m. The discrepancy increases with inferred dust attenuation, indicating that dust energy balance suffers from line-of-sight effects in systems with complex dust geometries. We find that adding NIRSpec spectroscopy to the fits breaks parameter degeneracies and strongly reduces the overprediction. When fitting the measured MIRI photometry together with the HST and NIRCam data, the best-fit model spectra of dusty galaxies ($A_V\gtrsim1$) result in significantly lower infrared luminosities by -0.6 dex compared to best-fit spectra obtained without MIRI, consistent with steeper, SMC-like attenuation curves or complex star-dust geometries. Our study highlights the limitations of dust energy balance at high redshift and underlines the importance of direct observations for accurately recovering the ISM and dust properties of galaxies at cosmic noon.

title: The THESAN-ZOOM project: interpreting candidate Population III-enriched absorption line systems during reionization
summary: With JWST, metal absorption lines are now being detected at increasingly high redshift, where signatures of the first generation of stars (Population III) may be observable. Interpreting observations of possible Pop III-enriched gas is challenging, as metals released by stars inevitably mix with pristine gas accreting onto galaxies and recycled gas from different episodes of star formation. Inference of Pop III enrichment from low-ionisation absorption lines requires placing stellar nucleosynthesis yields within the broader context of galaxy evolution. With THESAN-ZOOM, a set of high-resolution radiation hydrodynamical zoom-in simulations of galaxies, we investigate the metal abundance patterns observable in absorption. As our fiducial simulations do not include Pop III enrichment channels, our primary goal is to test how galaxy formation processes can shape observed abundance ratios. Our results indicate that a single abundance ratio plane, such as the commonly used [Si/O] vs. [C/O], cannot conclusively distinguish Pop III enrichment from enrichment by subsequent populations of stars. Robust detections instead require characterising multiple abundance ratios. In our simulations, a larger dispersion in abundance ratio distributions (often interpreted as possible evidence of pollution from the first stellar populations) naturally arises with increasing redshift, when the metallicity and dust content are lower. However, this alone does not reproduce all the observed results. By running an additional simulation with an updated THESAN-ZOOM model containing Pop III stars, we show that this has a large impact on the simulated abundance ratios, pushing them closer to those observed in potential Pop III-enriched gas.

title: Drilling for the Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland (RNO-G): field performance of BigRAID
summary: The Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland (RNO-G) is designed to detect ultra-high-energy neutrinos by capturing the radio signals generated when these rare particles interact with glacial ice. Located near Summit Station on the Greenland ice sheet, RNO-G will ultimately consist of 35 autonomous stations, each spaced 1.25 km apart and equipped with arrays of in-ice antennas. A key component of each station is a set of three subsurface strings of antennas, which require boreholes that are approximately 100 meters deep and more than 285 mm wide in diameter. Construction of the observatory began in 2021, and eight stations have been deployed to date. To meet the drilling requirements, the project utilizes the BigRAID system. Developed through a collaboration between the University of Wisconsin-Madison, the British Antarctic Survey (BAS), and the RNO-G Collaboration, BigRAID is being continually refined to improve its reliability, enhance drilling speed, and incorporate advanced automation and control software. This paper will review recent upgrades to the drill and assess its performance in the field through the four seasons of drilling.

title: Multiwavelength Analysis of the Merging Cluster RM J121917.6+505432.8: A Three-way Merger in Disguise?
summary: We identify the galaxy cluster RM J121917.6+505432.8 as a candidate bimodal merging cluster due to its optical properties listed in the redMaPPer cluster catalog. To confirm the cluster's merging state and reveal its dark matter halo and intracluster medium (ICM) morphologies, we conducted a multiwavelength follow-up campaign encompassing HST/ACS optical observations, XMM-Newton X-ray imaging, and Keck/Deimos multislit spectroscopy. The weak lensing mass reconstruction performed with the HST images shows two resolved peaks whose positions coincide with the two brightest cluster galaxies. The ICM morphology is consistent with a post-pericenter merger, with significant asymmetry in X-ray flux between subclusters. Our Keck/Deimos redshift measurements reveal a relative velocity $Δv_{\mathrm{LOS}} = 480$ km s$^{-1}$ between eastern and western subclusters. The eastern, more massive subcluster, however, exhibits a highly elongated shape, suggesting either a dark matter halo of considerable eccentricity or the presence of a third, unresolved halo, eliciting the question of whether RMJ1219 is truly binary or a three-way merger. To investigate these hypotheses, we fit the weak lensing shear data using four different combinations of spherical and elliptical NFW halo models and provide an estimate of the mass and concentration of each subhalo. Although the best fit is achieved with a three-halo model, the data are insufficient to determine whether the introduction of extra parameters is statistically justified.

title: Small-scale priors for large-scale cosmology: the case of $b_φ$
summary: Perturbative descriptions of galaxy clustering introduce free bias parameters that capture the complex physics of galaxy formation. Local primordial non-Gaussianity (PNG), parametrized by $f_{NL}$, induces a scale-dependent contribution to the galaxy bias that is proportional to $f_{NL} b_φ$, where $b_φ$ quantifies how galaxy formation responds to PNG. Accurately determining $b_φ$ is therefore essential for robust constraints on $f_{NL}$. Current analyses usually adopt a modified universal relation, $b_φ= 2δ_c(b_1-p)$, with $p$ calibrated to simulations. This relies on the accuracy of the simulated galaxy-formation model and ignores the uncertainty on $b_φ$, potentially biasing $f_{NL}$ constraints. We investigate whether $b_φ$ can be constrained from small-scale galaxy clustering using a flexible empirical galaxy-formation model. We fit an extended Subhalo Abundance Matching (SHAMe) model to small-scale clustering measurements and combine it with dark-matter-only separate-universe simulations to infer a posterior on $b_φ$. We validate the method using IllustrisTNG hydrodynamical separate-universe simulations. Without calibration on hydrodynamical simulations, SHAMe predicts $b_φ$ with a median error of 10%, compared with 38% for a fixed halo occupation distribution (HOD) that neglects the occupation response to $φ$, and 23% for the universality relation. The residual error is dominated by central galaxies near the selection threshold and persists when using the true stellar-mass assignment conditioned on the same subhalo properties. Small-scale clustering combined with a subhalo-based empirical model predicts most of galaxy-abundance response to local PNG. The remainder depends on galaxy-formation physics and should enter $b_φ$ priors as a theoretical uncertainty. This provides a route to data-informed priors on bias parameters.

title: High-Precision Photometry with a scientific CMOS Camera: III Lab and on-Sky testing of Andor Toran-26B
summary: Scientific CMOS cameras are increasingly used in modern astronomy, offering CCD-like performance with lower power use, faster readout, and reduced cost. We evaluate the photometric precision of the Toran-26B camera, featuring the IMX571 sensor from Sony, a new CMOS camera from Andor Technology, through laboratory and on-sky tests in its two modes: high well capacity (HWC) and low noise (LN). Key metrics include read noise, dark current, photo and dark signal non-uniformity, quantum efficiency, and window transmittance. The median read noise is 1.07\,e$^-$ (LN) and 2.79\,e$^-$ (HWC). Bias shows minor dark signal non-uniformity: 0.076\,e$^-$ (LN), 0.173\,e$^-$ (HWC). Pixel well depth reaches 15700\,e$^-$ (LN) and 50000\,e$^-$ (HWC), with dynamic ranges of 83.39\,dB and 85.05\,dB, respectively. Linearities are 99.93\,\% (LN) and 99.82\,\% (HWC) within the 5-95\,\% range of the saturation signal. Photo response non-uniformity is 0.076\,\% (LN) and 0.05\,\% (HWC). Dark current at 0\,$^\circ$C is 0.001\,\eps, (LN and HWC). On-sky tests show that, for our test telescope configuration, the HWC mode can be camera noise limited for specific magnitude ranges, while the LN mode remains free of such limitations, making it the preferred choice.

title: Physical quasar pairs in DESI DR1 as tracers of protoclusters at $z\approx2$
summary: Close pairs of quasars at the same redshift are expected to mark overdense regions that will collapse into galaxy clusters. Earlier work with SDSS found about 2800 such pairs, too few to follow their environment with separation. We build the largest sample of physical quasar pairs to date from DESI DR1 and test whether pairs out to Mpc separations trace protoclusters. We select pairs with rest-frame velocity difference $|ΔV|\leq900 km/s$ and projected separation $r_p\leq4$~Mpc at $1.2\leq z\leq2.8$, measure their purity and fibre completeness, and measure the clustering of pair members around all DESI quasars. We find 40\,626 physical pairs with projected separation $r_p\leq2.5$~Mpc, where their purity falls to 50\%, the effective radius of protoclusters at $z\approx2$. Pair members are $1.69\pm0.14$, $1.78\pm0.09$ and $2.01\pm0.06$ times more clustered than all quasars for projected separations $r_p\leq1$, 1--2.5 and 2.5--4~Mpc, while chance pairs show little excess ($1.08\pm0.05$). This corresponds to haloes of $\sim1.4$--$2.2\times10^{13}\,h^{-1}M_\odot$. Physical quasar pairs with projected separations up to 2.5~Mpc trace protocluster environments, at the level that AbacusSummit mocks predict in $Λ$CDM. The full DESI survey will turn them into a statistical census of protoclusters at cosmic noon.

title: A Genetic Algorithm Approach to Reconstructing Scalar-Tensor Lagrangians
summary: Recent DESI baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data, combined with cosmic microwave background (CMB) and Type Ia supernovae observations, have been interpreted as evidence for dynamical dark energy whose equation of state crosses the phantom divide $w=-1$. Such a crossing cannot be realized smoothly by a minimally coupled scalar field $\varphi$, but can arise naturally in scalar-tensor theories. We present a data-driven framework that reconstructs the scalar-tensor Lagrangian directly from observations, using a genetic algorithm to evolve the symbolic expressions for the nonminimal coupling $F(\varphi)$ and the scalar potential $U(\varphi)$. Each candidate is evaluated through a forward model that self-consistently determines the expansion history, the effective gravitational coupling, and the growth of structure. Candidates are ranked by a joint likelihood of DESI DR2 BAO, Pantheon+ supernovae calibrated with SH0ES Cepheids, compressed CMB distance priors, and redshift-space distortion measurements of $fσ_8$. We restrict to the unscreened branch of the theory and impose Solar System constraints on the post-Newtonian parameter $γ$ and on the time variation of the gravitational coupling, together with a Big Bang nucleosynthesis bound on its evolution. Across 64 independent runs, the best reconstruction improves the fit relative to $Λ$CDM by $Δχ^2=-16.6$, compared with $Δχ^2=-10.6$ for the CPL dark-energy parametrization. The preferred coupling is well described by $F(\varphi)=c_1\varphi^2+e^{\varphi}(1-c_2\varphi)$. The reconstructed theory shows phantom behavior at $z\gtrsim0.5$, but it remains close to $w=-1$ at low redshift.

title: Binary mass transfer fossil in the ancient GD-1 stellar stream
summary: We report the discovery of J0930+2902, the first carbon-enhanced metal-poor star with s-process enrichment (CEMP-s) identified in the GD-1 stellar stream, which is widely believed to originate from the tidal disruption of an old, metal-poor globular cluster. Using high-resolution Subaru/HDS spectroscopy, we present a comprehensive chemical abundance analysis of this star. Stellar atmospheric parameters were re-derived using Gaia photometry and parallaxes, combined with an iterative non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) analysis of Fe lines. We determine abundances for 22 elements, including NLTE analyses of C, Na, Mg, Ca, Ti, Cr, Mn, Co, Sr, Y, Zr, Ba, and Eu. J0930+2902 exhibits pronounced enhancements of C, N, Na, and s-process elements, together with a low $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C ratio of 7.4, consistent with enrichment through binary mass transfer from a former asymptotic giant branch (AGB) companion. Large radial-velocity variations and a significant near-ultraviolet excess independently indicate the presence of a white dwarf companion, providing strong support for this scenario. Comparisons with FRUITY AGB nucleosynthesis models show that the residual neutron-capture abundance pattern is best reproduced by a low-mass AGB companion with an initial mass of approximately 3.0 $M_{\odot}$. Its enhancements of C, N, Na, and s-process elements make it chemically distinct from the other confirmed GD-1 members. These results identify J0930+2902 as a fossil record of binary mass transfer preserved in the ancient GD-1 stellar stream, demonstrating that binary interaction can leave long-lived chemical signatures in accreted stellar populations.

title: OSIRIS-REx Lessons Learned Report: Insights from the Journey to Bennu and Back
summary: OSIRIS-REx, NASA's third New Frontiers mission, was the first U.S. mission to return a sample from an asteroid. Proposed in 2010 for an \$811 million lifecycle cost, the mission was completed for \$828 million, returned more than \$52 million of Headquarters reserves unused, and delivered at least 121.6 g of pristine material from near-Earth asteroid (101955) Bennu in September 2023, more than twice the Level-1 requirement. It did so despite a surface far more rugged than predicted, the discovery of particle ejection, sampling in a regolith much weaker than expected, operations during the COVID-19 pandemic, and an off-nominal parachute sequence on Earth return. This report sets out the lessons learned by the mission's leadership across six areas: leadership and governance; cost, schedule and risk management; systems engineering; mission operations; sample return, curation and analysis; and data archiving. Recurring themes are that a PI-led structure integrating science, engineering and project management gives the discipline to make fast, informed decisions; that reserves and schedule margin spent early to retire risk, such as funding Natural Feature Tracking as a backup navigation system, buy the flexibility to absorb discovery; that heritage hardware reduces risk only when its verification and engineering knowledge are preserved; and that contamination knowledge, sample science and data stewardship are mission-long responsibilities, not post-flight tasks. Each section pairs background with specific recommendations for future sample-return and small-body missions.

title: UNIONS and Euclid: Calibrating point source-galaxy separation for ground-based surveys
summary: Efficient separation of unresolved point sources from extended objects (star-galaxy separation) is essential for deep wide-field imaging surveys, particularly at faint magnitudes where morphological differences become subtle. We assess two morphology-based classification methods applied to single-band, ground-based imaging from the Ultraviolet Near-Infrared Optical Northern Survey (UNIONS), using Euclid observations as a high-fidelity reference to evaluate their performance and to train one of the methods. We analysed 8 deg$^2$ of overlapping UNIONS $r$-band and Euclid $I_E$ data, comprising more than $7\times10^{5}$ sources. The Euclid data enable robust morphological labelling down to $I_E\simeq 26$, which we used to train and validate two classification approaches applied to UNIONS alone: a curve-of-growth method and a supervised neural-network classifier, both based on aperture photometry and image-quality information. The curve-of-growth method yields an almost perfectly complete point-source sample ($>95\%$), but its purity decreases rapidly at $r \simeq 22.5$. The neural-network approach significantly improves the purity at the faint end, maintaining $\geq 80\%$ purity down to $r \simeq 24$, while the completeness decreases to almost $50\%$ at similar depths. In both cases, performance strongly depends on the image quality of the ground-based data. This work shows how Euclid data can be used to develop, calibrate, and validate star-galaxy separation methods for ground-based surveys, useful in regions not covered by Euclid. Both methods have already been applied to UNIONS data and are readily applicable to future surveys such as LSST, offering flexible solutions depending on whether completeness or purity is prioritised.

title: Beyond the blur: Radial binning trumps stellar migration in resolved star formation histories
summary: Spatially resolved galaxy properties are routinely derived from integral-field spectroscopy and increasingly from multi-band photometry as a wealth of photometric data become available in large surveys like LSST/Rubin. Spatially resolved star formation histories (SFHs) offer a detailed view of galaxy growth and quenching by tracing the timing and location of star formation within a galaxy up to one billion years in the past. However, stellar migration between spaxels may strongly bias these reconstructions. Quantifying this bias remains challenging as few Milky-Way mass simulations fully resolve initial stellar dispersions or migration rates. We use the well-validated h277 Milky-Way-mass cosmological zoom simulation, which resolves both via explicitly tying star formation to the non-equilibrium abundance of H2, to assess the quality of specific star formation rates (sSFR) radial profiles inferred from resolved SFHs against actual values from stellar particle tracking. Across several evolutionary windows spanning a range of stellar activity stages from quiescent to star-bursting, we find that the adaptive radial binning imposed by S/N constraints in photometric SED fitting actually mitigates most of the blurring/mixing effects of stellar migration on inferred radial profiles up to lookback times of 1.5 Gyr. This allows for proper recovery of not only the average sSFR but also its radial slope, its relative changes in scatter across radial annuli and even approximate localization of low-z star-forming clumps. Only galaxies having undergone a major merger across the considered lookback time display discrepant, unreliable sSFR profiles, hence should not be considered for such reconstructions.

title: Constraining Intergalactic Dust with Supernova Color Evolution: Current Constraints from DES and Forecasts for LSST and Roman
summary: Dust is an important systematic in precision Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) cosmology, and while dust in the Milky Way and SN host galaxies has been extensively studied, the impact of potential intergalactic dust is less well constrained. Using estimates from B. Ménard et al. (2010), we find that current intergalactic dust bounds could shift SN distance moduli by up to 0.02 mag at $z \gtrsim 1$ from simulations. However, we show dust models can be constrained independently by SN samples themselves via a specific predicted redshift-dependent evolution observed in SN colors. While current data from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) cannot distinguish between various amounts of intergalactic dust in our universe, we demonstrate that the Roman Space Telescope (Roman) will place a significant constraint on intergalactic dust models ($>$ 3$σ$). In contrast, the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), even with its unprecedented statistics, will only reach $\lesssim$ 2$σ$ significance on any given intergalactic dust prediction relative to no dust. We propagate multiple parameterizations of intergalactic dust through to cosmology. For LSST, we see a $\sim$60% reduction in the figure of merit (FoM) for $w$CDM and a $\sim$20% reduction for $w_0w_a$CDM, and for Roman, a $\sim$20% reduction in the FoM for $w$CDM and a $\sim$5% reduction for $w_0w_a$CDM. Utilizing Roman as an external constraint on dust for LSST results in a slightly improved FoM ($\sim$50% reduction) for $w$CDM for LSST. Finally, we show that intergalactic dust uncertainties decrease the FoM of the previous DES analysis (16.9% for $w$CDM and 8.1% for $w_0w_a$CDM) and that intergalactic dust cannot explain away recent hints for evolving dark energy.

title: Black hole accretion flows as dark matter bolometers
summary: Astrophysical systems provide powerful probes of dark matter interactions, complementing direct-detection searches. We propose using accretion flows of the supermassive black hole as a bolometer for light DM. The kinetic energy of sub-MeV dark matter in the black hole gravitational potential can remain below the thermal energy of the plasma electrons. The colder dark matter population can therefore absorb energy through elastic scattering, cooling the electrons and modifying their emission spectrum. We integrate dark matter cooling into the advection-dominated accretion flow around M87$^{*}$ and solve the full set of thermodynamic equations to obtain the resulting temperature profile and radio-to-millimeter emission. By comparing the predicted spectrum with observations accompanying the Event Horizon Telescope campaign, we use, for the first time, the thermal energy balance of the hot accretion flow to constrain DM-electron scattering, obtaining stringent limits on keV-to-MeV DM for both heavy and light mediators.

title: Galaxy cluster thermodynamic profiles beyond self-similarity
summary: Galaxy cluster formation is a self-similar and scale-free process of gravitational collapse. However, the thermodynamic properties of the intracluster medium often deviate from self-similar predictions. We investigate these deviations using a sample of 92 galaxy clusters selected through their Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect signal, spanning a mass range of $M_{500c}=[0.5-20] \times 10^{14}{M}_{\odot}$, and with redshifts $0.08 < z < 1.13$. Adopting a flexible framework that allows for radial variations in both redshift and mass scaling, we characterise the behaviour of scaled density, temperature, pressure, and entropy profiles, while simultaneously constraining their intrinsic scatter. We detect significant radial deviations from self-similar expectations in both redshift and mass scalings in all profiles. These deviations are strongest in the core regions, but remain measurable out to large radii ($\sim R_{500c}$), indicating that cluster outer regions are not fully described by purely gravitational evolution. We investigate the impact of an offset, a mass-dependence, and increased scatter between the mass proxy and the true mass on the radial mass scaling, finding that while its shape remains stable, its normalisation depends on the latter two effects. The pressure is the only thermodynamic quantity that exhibits approximately self-similar behaviour: outside the core it evolves self-similarly, with no dependence on mass. The entropy exhibits the strongest deviations from self-similarity as a function of radius. The intrinsic scatter peaks in the central regions and reaches a minimum at intermediate radii ($\lesssim 20 \%$ at $\sim 0.2$-$0.8 \ R_{500c}$), making this range optimal to reduce scatter in scaling relations. We conclude that the thermodynamic distributions exhibit non-self similar, mass-dependent scaling extending well beyond the core regime.

title: Scaling and Cross-Simulation Generalization of Graph Neural Networks for Cosmic-Web Classification in CAMELS
summary: Graph-based methods can classify galaxies by their dark-matter cosmic-web environments, but reliability beyond development simulations remains uncertain. Galaxy-formation models alter tracer populations and spatial distributions, potentially shifting graph features. We test how graph neural networks scale with independent training realizations and transfer across hydrodynamical simulations. Using the $z=0$ CAMELS IllustrisTNG, SIMBA and Astrid suites, we label galaxies with $M_\star>10^9\,M_\odot$ as void, sheet, filament or knot from the smoothed cold-dark-matter density field. We represent their spatial distributions as periodic Delaunay graphs with ten geometric descriptors. We compare a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and five graph neural networks (GNNs), including a local graph Transformer, under realization-grouped evaluation. Learning curves increase training data from 10 to 100 realizations, with validation and test boxes fixed. We test every source-to-target suite pairing on 100 unseen realizations per target suite. On this external holdout, the Transformer, GAT+ and EdgeConv reach mean per-realization macro-averaged F1 scores of $0.652$, $0.651$ and $0.642$, against $0.481$ for the MLP. The Transformer outperforms the MLP by 0.171, while the difference between the Transformer and GAT+ is not statistically significant. Voids remain the hardest class. Performance is higher in boxes with more selected galaxies and shorter Delaunay edges. Associations with cosmological and feedback parameters weaken after accounting for galaxy richness and void fraction. Our results benchmark the scaling and cross-simulation transfer of galaxy-graph classifiers, demonstrating the value of neighbourhood information and identifying tracer sampling as an important limitation for dark-matter web inference.

title: Curvature Mismatch and Local Errors in Galaxy Property Estimation
summary: Linear probes are widely used to evaluate learned representations and infer physical quantities from unlabelled data. The probe's predictions are from an affine function in ambient space restricted to the underlying representation, and consequently, even a representation that has complete information needed to predict a target can produce systematic probe errors when that information is encoded in a form inaccessible to the linear probe. Here we share that some of this probing error is due to the innate geometry of the manifold. Linear probes, when evaluated on a curved manifold, generally have a nonzero intrinsic Hessian (what we colloquially call "probe-facing curvature") given by $\langle w_N,\mathrm{II}\rangle$, the manifold's second fundamental form dotted with the probe's normal component. We fit linear probes to galaxy embeddings from five pretrained encoders and intervene on this curvature term to evaluate its contribution to the probe performance. We find that keeping this inherited curvature improves the local fit where it matches the label's curvature. Removing the curvature component of the probe where it does not match the label curvature also provides improvements, and correcting it in every neighbourhood raises held-out local $R^2$ by 0.006 to 0.010 on galaxies, gaining more where the two curvatures disagree. We isolated these gains to be from the underlying geometry and not an automatic guarantee from least squares training.

title: A Bayesian Approach to Prioritizing the Follow-Up of Near-Earth Objects
summary:
We present pneo, a Bayesian classifier that computes the probability that a single-night tracklet belongs to a near-Earth object (NEO), using only its sky position, angular motion, and apparent magnitude. A tracklet does not determine the object's distance or radial velocity, so pneo integrates a model of the Solar System's small-body populations over all bound orbits consistent with it. The result is the exact posterior probability under that model, with no tuned scores or separately chosen priors: its classifications are optimal for the adopted model, and its probabilities are calibrated.
  On real discovery tracklets from the NEO Confirmation Page, the classifier is well calibrated and its selection is 1.14 times purer than that of digest2, the classifier now in use, at the same completeness. The advantage grows at Rubin's depth, where the faint background of main-belt and more distant objects is still largely undiscovered. On simulated tracklets to that depth, its selection is 2 times purer than that of digest2 (96% against 48%). On the Rubin alert stream and Rubin Data Preview 2 its selection is 1.4-1.7 times purer than that of digest2, and its predicted NEO counts are close to those observed. By raising the fraction of follow-up targets that are NEOs, pneo could potentially double the effective capacity of NEO follow-up in the Rubin era.

title: periapsis: A Comprehensive Orbital Fitting Package
summary: We introduce a new Python package \texttt{periapsis}, which computes posterior distributions for a variety of orbital parameters given astrometric and/or radial velocity data. \texttt{periapsis} not only returns posterior distributions, but also a variety of statistics assessing convergence and fit metrics as well as plotting capabilities for visualizing the orbital systems. In this paper, we describe our various methods for fitting Keplerian orbits to both astrometric and radial velocity data. We then show the breadth of binary systems that \texttt{periapsis} can characterize by comparing our computed parameters with known orbital systems. Finally, we discuss how \texttt{periapsis} will be a helpful tool for future data releases like \textit{Gaia} DR4 and \textit{Roman}.

title: Black holes in little red and blue dots drive no superwinds in the first 1.5 billion years
summary: Galaxy-formation models rely on accreting black holes to expel gas from their hosts. We test this prediction in 67 little red dots (LRDs) and little blue dots (LBDs) in the first 1.5 billion years, selected from 80,367 NIRSpec spectra in the DAWN JWST Archive. We detect no [O III] wind, against lower limits of 7.2 and 7.5 expected detections for local sub-Eddington and super-Eddington active nuclei. For winds narrower than 1,500 km/s, the corresponding incidence limits are 13% and 19% at 95% confidence, compared with 31% and 49% locally. Broad Balmer lines are centred on the narrow lines, and Balmer absorbers move below 8% of the escape speed. Published super-Eddington fountain, black-hole-star and quasi-star models each fail a measured property of the spectra. LRDs and LBDs drive no superwinds, and their black holes grow without the wind feedback invoked to regulate galaxies.

title: A search and multi-frequency study of curved parsec-scale jets in active galaxies
summary: Very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations show that a fraction of active galactic nucleus (AGN) jets exhibit pronounced apparent bending on parsec scales, potentially strongly enhanced by projection effects. While individual sources have been studied in detail, the statistical properties of curved jets and the physical mechanisms responsible for their morphology remain poorly constrained. We aim to select a statistically robust sample of AGNs with significantly curved parsec-scale jets and to constrain the physical mechanisms responsible for jet bending. We analyse 123 456 VLBI images of 17 478 AGNs collected by the public Astrogeo database. After filtering for extended structure, we extract and stack multi-epoch, multi-frequency (1.2--86 GHz) ridge lines. We fit linear and logarithmic helices representing jet precession and resonant Kelvin--Helmholtz instability mode. We combine model-fits and Monte Carlo simulations to further constrain these physical models. We robustly identify 586 AGNs (7.4% of sources with resolved jets) with curved parsec-scale jets. Compared to straight jets, curved ones are less common at low redshifts, possibly due to the sample-related selection effects. In the precession scenario, the inferred periods span $P \sim$10--10 000 yr, with a logarithmic mean of $\sim 220$ yr. Solid-body disc precession in supermassive black hole binaries is broadly consistent with these periods, whereas geodetic precession requires extremely tight, near-equal-mass systems. Lense--Thirring precession remains viable for both thin and thick discs. Kelvin--Helmholtz instability also provides a potential explanation. However, identifying the preferred model for each individual source requires further investigation, including temporal analysis and jet kinematics.

title: Environmental resonances in extreme-mass-ratio inspirals within boson clouds
summary: Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) offer a promising probe of matter environments around massive black holes through gravitational-wave (GW) observations. We investigate orbital resonances induced by conservative gravitational perturbations from such environments. Combining a multiparameter expansion with the action-angle formalism, we derive a general resonance condition for generic bound Kerr orbits. Applying this framework to ultralight scalar clouds formed through black hole superradiance, we show that orbital resonances can arise from a single-mode cloud without requiring transitions between cloud modes. Our analysis demonstrates that these resonances can lead to significant GW dephasing, providing a new avenue for probing boson clouds through GWs and highlighting the importance of including environmental resonances in accurate EMRI waveform modeling.

title: Moon Radio Interferometer for Science and Exploration (MoonRISE): A Mission Concept for a Low-Frequency Radio Interferometer on the Lunar Farside
summary: The universe below 20 MHz remains one of space science's last unexplored frontiers, inaccessible from Earth due to its ionosphere and terrestrial radio frequency interference (RFI). We present the mission concept for the Moon Radio Interferometer for Science and Exploration (MoonRISE), an all-sky imaging, low-frequency radio telescope operating from 100 kHz-30 MHz from the lunar farside, the quietest radio environment in the inner Solar System. If realized, MoonRISE would be the first radio interferometer on the Moon and the first connected-element radio interferometer in space. Its science objectives are to (1) determine how solar wind turbulence drives plasma heating, acceleration, and space weather evolution in the inner heliosphere, by measuring the scattering of type III solar radio bursts between 2-20 solar radii; (2) constrain the density, structure, and variability of the lunar ionosphere and its effects on surface communication; and (3) resolve the plasma sources and magnetospheric dynamics that power Uranian Kilometric Radiation, observable for the first time since Voyager 2 in 1986. The same observations would yield all-sky maps of the low-frequency sky, subsurface structure at the landing site, and a characterization of the farside RF environment. The Radio Interferometer concept consists of nine 3.5 m dipoles embedded in a 1.5 km optical-fiber tether deployed by a rover, with power- and RF-over-fiber enabling RFI-free mapping. A rover-mounted Ground Penetrating Radar (300-2000 MHz) would measure regolith dielectric properties and bedrock depth to characterize the dipoles' RF performance. We describe the science objectives, a reference landing site in Lacus Luxuriae, a notional concept of operations, and the payload design and technology maturity. The concept builds on SunRISE and OVRO-LWA heritage and could serve as a basis for a future selected mission.

title: Low-latency gravitational wave alert infrastructure and new data products for multi-messenger astronomy during LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA's fourth observing run
summary: Multi-messenger investigations of compact object mergers, such as binary neutron star and neutron star-black hole systems, remain among the most dynamic frontiers of modern astronomy. During the fourth observing run of Advanced LIGO, Advanced Virgo, and KAGRA, the search for joint electromagnetic and neutrino counterparts to gravitational-wave signals continued using public, semi-automated data products distributed in near real-time. The sky localizations and preliminary source characterizations provided by these alerts helped guide multiple rapid follow-up observations to candidate gravitational-wave events. During this run, the low-latency search parameter space was expanded to include the sub-solar mass regime and associated public data products were developed. Further, chirp mass estimates of the binary merger system were introduced as a new public data product and distributed to enable follow-up searches to concentrate their resources on the most promising transients. In order to streamline the implementation of new searches and data products, a mock data challenge, known as the Low-Latency Production Integration Challenge (LLPIC), was used as a replay of a simulated population of gravitational-wave sources to optimize and profile the software infrastructure and scientific deliverables. In this paper we describe these new public data products, their performance and the result of end-to-end testing of the low-latency infrastructure with the LLPIC.

title: First detection of s-cis-acroleine (sc-CH2CHCHO) in the interstellar medium
summary: We report the first interstellar detection of the higher-energy $s$-cis conformer of acrolein (CH2CHCHO) toward TMC-1 using the Quijote line survey. Local thermodynamic equilibrium modeling, assuming a rotational temperature of 7.5 K, yields a column density of $(1.0\pm0.2)\times10^{11}$~cm$^{-2}$ when fitting the observed lines. The s-cis/s-trans abundance ratio is $0.45\pm0.11$, despite an energy separation of approximately 1025~K, indicating a strongly nonequilibrium conformational distribution. An exploratory gas--grain chemical model identifies C3H5 + O as the dominant acrolein formation route, pointing to this reaction as a first entry to consider when explaining the isomeric ratios. The observed ratio provides a new constraint on conformer-specific formation, destruction, and interconversion processes in cold interstellar clouds.

title: First Order Real Resonant Digital Filters and A Novel Orthogonal State Generator
summary: We describe FOREST, a real, first order digital resonant filter and orthogonal state generator. We show that in spite of the imaginary nature of the roots of the transfer function of a resonator, appropriate interpretation of this transfer function nonetheless leads to a practical first order filter with real coefficients. We use a discrete state space model of FOREST to predict the resonator properties, and implement the filter in digital signal processing slices on a digital signal processing platform. Applications are in real time digital signal processing, engineering fields such as mains electricity monitoring and motor control, any application requiring a phase locked loop, and physics applications utilising high-quality-factor resonators.

title: Comprehensive In Situ Characterization of Amorphous Solid Water Films with COSPINU2 set-up: Optical Properties, Density, Morphology, and Restructuring Dynamics
summary: Amorphous solid water (ASW) dominates interstellar ice mantles, but its porosity, density, optical response, and mechanical stability depend sensitively on how the ice is grown. Here, we present the characterization capabilities of COSPINU2, a cryogenic ultra-high-vacuum set-up designed to prepare and diagnose water ice films under controlled background and doser-assisted deposition conditions. The instrument combines a calibrated gas-handling line, near- and mid-infrared Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, HeNe interferometry, broad-beam optical imaging, and quadrupole mass spectrometry. We demonstrate how these complementary diagnostics provide a coherent description of ASW films grown between 10K and 150K. For background-grown ices, a dual-angle interferometric method is used to retrieve refractive indices near 632 nm, while near-infrared interference fringes provide thickness calibration. The results show that lower deposition temperatures and higher growth rates produce films with lower refractive indices and stronger dangling-OH infrared signatures, consistent with the formation of more porous ASW. We also show that pressure-based density estimates are unreliable in the background geometry because cryopumping decouple chamber pressure from the local substrate flux. For doser-grown films, optical interference imaging allows reconstruction of dome-shaped thickness profiles and estimation of effective densities. Finally, sudden restructuring events are observed in thick (above 2 micrometers), low-temperature porous ASW films, evidenced by abrupt changes in interferometric contrast, optical scattering, and dangling-OH features. These results establish COSPINU2 as a versatile platform for quantitative water-ice characterization and provide the physical baseline required for future studies of infrared irradiation and optical constants of interstellar ice analogues.

title: Azimuth Pointing and Momentum Management for a Lightweight High-Altitude Balloon Payload
summary: The ALTAIR (Airborne Laser for Telescopic Atmospheric Interference Reduction) project provides photometric calibration for ground-based telescopes by flying an integrating sphere as an artificial star-like calibration source on a high-altitude balloon. Because the angular distribution of light from the exit port of the sphere is approximately Lambertian, the payload must keep its azimuth within $\pm8^\circ$ of the telescope line of sight. This condition bounds the fractional difference in light intensity from that along the exit-port normal to below 1%. The bound must be held for at least 30 s at a time. This paper presents a pointing architecture that combines passive stabilization, onboard attitude determination, and active azimuth control using a momentum wheel, with active desaturation through a second motor at the flight-train pivot. Carbon-fiber inertial booms reduce off-axis pendulating motion sufficiently for azimuth control to be treated independently. Attitude is determined by onboard fusion of rate gyro, accelerometer, magnetometer, and dual-antenna GNSS carrier-phase measurements. A high-fidelity simulation of the payload, including motor dynamics and limits, sensor noise, and wind disturbances generated from flight data, is used to size actuators and tune the control loops. The payload avionics, flight software, power management, controls, and real-time ground telemetry systems are developed in-house. The system is evaluated through ground testing, simulation, and two flights. With the momentum wheel alone, 53 intervals of 30 s pointing within $\pm8^\circ$ of the target azimuth are recorded during ascent, with a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of $3.7^\circ$, and the longest uninterrupted window lasts 7 min 55 s with $5^\circ$ of pointing RMSE. Simulation results suggest significant performance improvements from adding a pivot motor for momentum management.

title: Modeling time series of high-resolution spectra using the asymmetric Hilbert-Schmidt decomposition with application to radial velocity exoplanet searches
summary: We describe a framework for building low-rank separable expansions to model spectroscopic data from systems with time-varying spectra, in settings where the spectral dimension is finely sampled (in wavelength), but the temporal dimension is sparsely and possibly irregulary sampled. The motivating application is detection and characterization of small exoplanets, e.g., Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars. Such planets cannot be seen directly, but can be detected via the minute Doppler shifts of the host star spectrum due to the star's motion as the planet and star revolve around their mutual center of mass. Current instruments are reaching the precision necessary to detect the ~10 cm/s motions corresponding to an exo-Earth. But the small Doppler shifts from such low-amplitude orbital motion can be masked or mimicked by the effects of stellar activity on the surface of the host star. e.g., starspots (dark regions), faculae (bright filaments), etc. One technique astronomers have used to try to model the stellar activity component of the signal is PCA, applied to an ensemble of spectra collected over time. But PCA neglects the continuous function nature of a spectrum at a given time, and the continuous evolution of spectra over time. We address model building from a function approximation perspective, via the asymmetric Hilbert-Schmidt decomposition (HSD). This provides a PCA-like low-rank decomposition of a dynamic spectrum, but it explicitly accounts for time dependence, both estimating temporal basis functions, and accounting for irregular temporal sampling when estimating spectral basis functions. We show that HSD improves the fidelity of a fixed-order model of the dynamic spectrum of a Sun-like star with a starspot, with mean squared error for spectral basis functions many times smaller than achieved via PCA when spectra are randomly sampled sparsely and irregularly in time.

title: Less massive black holes in faint hosts: SED fitting of Little Red Dots within the Black Hole Star scenario
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a population of compact sources known as ``little red dots'' (LRDs), characterized by a distinctive V-shaped spectral energy distribution (SED) from UV to optical wavelengths. The physical nature of these sources remains debated. The ``black hole star'' (BH*) scenario, wherein a super-Eddington accreting black hole is embedded in a dense gaseous envelope, has been proposed to explain them. We assemble a sample of 22 LRDs at $4.0 \lesssim z \lesssim 9.5$ from the ASTRODEEP-JWST database. We construct a composite ``host galaxy + BH*'' model using the \texttt{Cloudy} photoionization code, and perform SED fitting with \textsc{BayeSED3}. Our modeling reproduces the observed V-shaped features: the UV continuum blueward of the Balmer break is well reproduced by stellar emission within this decomposition, while the optical regime is dominated by the BH* component. Our fits reveal that LRDs are black holes hosted by faint, low-mass galaxies with median stellar and black hole masses of $M_* = 10^{8.7}\,M_\odot$ and $M_{\rm BH} = 10^{6.4}\,M_\odot$, respectively. These black holes are moderately overmassive relative to local scaling relations but less extreme than broad-line estimates. The median bolometric luminosity $L_{\rm BH^*} \sim 10^{44.9}\,\rm erg\,s^{-1}$ mitigates the reported number density tension from 1--2 orders of magnitude to a factor of a few. The host galaxies lie near the high-redshift star-forming main sequence, and stellar extinction correlates positively with star formation rate (SFR). The BH* scenario provides a self-consistent paradigm for LRDs, offering insights into the rapid growth of supermassive black hole seeds and their co-evolution with host galaxies during the cosmic dawn.

title: RIFT for the O4 era: operating points, calibration marginalization, and cross-code validation
summary: The Rapid Iterative FiTting (RIFT) parameter inference algorithm provides a simulation-based-inference approach to efficient, highly-parallelized parameter inference for GW sources. In this paper, we describe improvements deployed during preparations for and analysis of O4 observations (versions 0.0.17.3--0.0.18.0) that broaden RIFT's reach for single-event inference with contemporary instruments. We provide additional options to increase compatibility and comparability with other codes, notably including (a) enhancing RIFT's capabilities for calibration marginalization; (b) managing our likelihood's internal, output, and time-interpolated representation; (c) introducing new coordinates for (transverse) spin and eccentric mean anomaly, enabling more robust inference of parameters with subtle and complex correlations to others, and (d) revised operating point choices better suited to the loudest, clearest signals. We identify and reconcile the most substantial sources of head-to-head likelihood differences between RIFT and other production inference codes, and describe automated waveform symmetry checks that detect upstream model regressions before they bias inference. Using the previously-reported RIFT/asimov interface for reproducible settings consistent with past work, we demonstrate these capabilities end to end.

title: The role of hierarchy in Galactic molecular clouds
summary: To probe the role of hierarchical gas structures in massive star formation, we statistically analyzed 13 Galactic massive star-forming regions using FUGIN CO survey data. Applying a non-binary dendrogram to the position-position-velocity data, we classified the extracted structures into trunks, internal leaves (the densest substructures within trunks), and isolated structures, and compared their properties with an analysis of variance controlling for regional differences. In representative regions, the trunks correspond to morphologies such as filaments and hub-filament systems, or to kinematic signatures of structure-forming events such as cloud-cloud collisions. Across the sample, the trunks are extended, massive, and strongly bound reservoirs, while the leaves are significantly more massive, denser, and more tightly bound than isolated structures of similar spatial scale. Using YSOs and Hi-GAL clumps, we find that the leaves have a lower low-mass star formation efficiency than isolated structures, whereas their clump formation efficiency is comparable. At a fixed gas mass, the leaves show no higher low-mass star formation efficiency than isolated structures but convert a larger fraction of their gas into dense clumps. We interpret these contrasts, together with inward gas motions in the position-velocity diagrams, as indicating that the deep potential of the trunks sustains continuous accretion onto the leaves and promotes mutual interactions among them. These processes may raise the characteristic fragmentation mass, as theoretically expected for a dynamically accreting medium, so that a larger fraction of the gas forms massive clumps without a corresponding increase in low-mass star formation. Our single-epoch data constrain only these structural contrasts, but indicate that the gas available for massive star formation is organized on scales larger than a single core.

title: PINN-Slicer: Exploiting Rotational Symmetry to Solve the Photon Orbit Equation Around a Black Hole
summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) typically struggle with long-horizon domains, often requiring the network to be retrained as the domain grows. We present PINN-Slicer, a method for second-order autonomous ordinary differential equations, $\ddot{u} = G(u, \dot{u})$, which exploits the invariance of this class of equations under translations of the independent variable. A single PINN, embedded within a solution ansatz that enforces the initial conditions explicitly, is trained on a thin slice of the independent variable using Sobol-sampled initial conditions. The PINN is then deployed recursively, slice-by-slice, across the full domain. We demonstrate PINN-Slicer on the nonlinear equation that describes photon orbits around a black hole, and reach a point-by-point root-mean-square error (RMSE) below $10^{-3}$ in $u = r_s/r$ (the inverse radial coordinate in units of the Schwarzschild radius) relative to a finite-difference reference solution. A key advantage of PINN-Slicer is that a single trained network generalizes to any orbital initial condition within the training range, without retraining. In addition, PINN-Slicer can cope with solution domains that may not be known a priori.

title: Bar Kinematics in Paired and Isolated Galaxies: Slow Bars Are More Likely Found in Paired Galaxies
summary: Bars are common structures in disk galaxies that can strongly influence the evolution of their hosts. Simulations predict that bars formed through tidal interactions tend to rotate slower than bars formed in isolation. We test this prediction observationally by studying the kinematics of 314 bars in galaxies between $0.016<z<0.130$. We use estimates of the bar pattern speed ($Ω_p$) and the rotation rate ($\mathcal{R}$) obtained from four studies using IFU data from the MaNGA survey. We cross-match the host galaxies of the bars to the Galaxy Zoo DESI catalogue in order to study their environment and classify each galaxy as paired or isolated. We find that bars that are slower in terms of $\mathcal{R}$ are more likely to be found in paired galaxies. The fraction of bars in paired galaxies increases from $5^{+6}_{-2}\%$ for $0<\mathcal{R}<1.0$ to $31^{+15}_{-9}\%$ for $3.0<\mathcal{R}<4.0$. Our results also suggest a possible difference in the distribution of $\mathcal{R}$ between paired (mean $\mathcal{R}=2.1 \pm 0.2$) and isolated (mean $\mathcal{R}=1.75 \pm 0.07$) galaxies (p-value=0.037; 2.09$σ$).
